title: 95% of Vietnamese Want Change: How Public Support Is Reshaping the Dog Trade
excerpt: New data from Hanoi shows 53 dog and cat meat facilities have closed or transitioned in just months. But the real story? Vietnamese citizens are leading this shift—95% support ending the trade entirely.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam is at a cultural inflection point. While 39 rabies deaths in the first half of 2026 underscore the public health crisis, the real momentum comes from Vietnamese citizens themselves: 95% of Vietnamese support eliminating the dog meat trade. In July 2026, Hanoi became the first proof of concept, with 53 facilities closing or registering for livelihood transition. This isn't imposed change—it's demanded change.

Key Findings

Hanoi's 53-Facility Shift: When Citizens Vote with Their Wallets

On July 24, 2026, Hanoi held the Fourth Livelihood Transition Training Conference, marking a watershed moment in Vietnam's dog meat debate. The headline figure tells the story: 28 dog and cat meat facilities had ceased operations, while 25 others registered to change business models. This isn't regulatory coercion—it's economic reality meeting consumer preference. The absence of demand is reshaping supply faster than any law could.

Giang Vo Ward became the first locality in the pilot area with zero operating dog and cat meat trading facilities, signaling that neighborhood-level transformation is possible. Traders aren't being arrested; they're being retrained into sustainable livelihoods, a model that respects both economic dignity and shifting public values.

The Health Crisis Driving the Cultural Shift: 39 Deaths, 24 Provinces

Vietnam recorded 39 human rabies deaths across 18 provinces and cities in the first half of 2026 alone, with animal rabies outbreaks confirmed in 24 provinces and cities. These aren't abstract statistics—they're neighbors, family members, preventable losses. This public health catastrophe has crystallized public opinion in ways that years of advocacy alone could not. When citizens see the direct link between an unregulated trade and rabies transmission, support for change becomes not just moral but existential.

Hanoi officials explicitly framed their livelihood transition project as integral to rabies prevention, food safety, and zoonotic disease reduction. The message: ending the dog meat trade isn't just about animal welfare—it's about protecting Vietnamese families from preventable disease.

Why 95% Vietnamese Support Matters More Than Any Ban

A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese citizens support ending the dog meat trade. That statistic has aged remarkably well—and Hanoi's July 2026 results suggest it may actually underestimate current sentiment. When a cultural practice loses the backing of 19 out of 20 citizens, it's no longer a tradition; it's a liability. The trade persists not because Vietnamese want it, but because it exists in regulatory shadow, untouched by enforcement, disconnected from public will.

What's shifting is visibility. On July 23, 2026, Dong Nai police intercepted a motorbike carrying five dogs and one dead cat destined for slaughter, originating from a pet-theft ring. These stories—once hidden—now reach Vietnamese households through phones and family conversations. Each exposure strengthens the 95%, transforming passive support into active demand for change.

Danang's Stray Management: Public Safety Meets Compassion

Parallel to Hanoi's trade reduction efforts, Danang launched a formalized stray dog and cat capture system on July 22, 2026, requiring 48-hour holding periods and proof of ownership for recovery. The framework includes provisions for unclaimed animals to transfer to research institutions or sanctuaries, rather than slaughter. This represents a quiet but profound semantic shift: from disposability to stewardship. Vietnamese cities are reframing strays as community members worthy of dignity, not inventory.

Also Worth Noting

  • Hanoi's pilot covers 14 wards with dedicated livelihood support — Traders aren't being left behind; they're being reskilled into sustainable occupations that don't depend on disappearing demand.
  • Gia Lai reports ongoing rabies risk from poor dog vaccination coverage — Provinces with weaker enforcement show the difference between aspirational policy and implemented protection.
  • Pet theft rings are being dismantled by police investigation — Criminal enforcement against trafficking is accelerating, signaling stronger political will to disrupt the supply chain.
  • Youth-led advocacy is reshaping generational attitudes in urban centers — Younger Vietnamese, especially in cities, increasingly reject the trade as incompatible with modern, humane society.

Take Action: The shift you're seeing in Hanoi, Danang, and across Vietnamese media isn't spontaneous—it's driven by citizens demanding change. Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030, and add your voice to the 95% of Vietnamese citizens already calling for this transformation.

When 95% of Vietnamese citizens agree on something, change isn't a question of if—it's a question of when.

July 2026 brought the proof: Hanoi closed 28 dog and cat meat facilities and transitioned 25 others to new livelihoods. Giang Vo Ward is now completely free of the trade. These aren't government raids—they're the market responding to what Vietnamese people actually want. A 2021 survey showed overwhelming public support for ending this trade, and that momentum is accelerating.

The health crisis is undeniable. 39 rabies deaths in the first half of 2026 alone. 24 provinces hit with animal outbreaks. Vietnamese citizens aren't just rejecting the trade on ethical grounds—they're protecting their families from preventable disease. Hanoi's livelihood transition program isn't punitive; it's supporting traders to build new, sustainable occupations. That's compassion at scale.

Cities like Danang are reimagining what it means to care for animals too. Stray dogs are now being held in shelters for 48 hours, with placement opportunities, not slaughter. A quiet revolution in how Vietnamese communities see their role.

This is Vietnamese-led change. These are Vietnamese voices. These are Vietnamese values reshaping the nation.
